summary.en: Ethan shares a simple but powerful reframe: you don't need many ideas to be seen as inventive—just one good idea every month or two, even if expressing it takes years (what he calls the long arc of Prime and Kindle). He tells a candid story of failing on a major project for Jeff Bezos and what it taught him, and walks through 'The Magic Loop,' a deceptively simple practice he guarantees will help you get promoted. The episode is full of concrete career advice for senior individual contributors and managers, including how to stand out in interviews and how Amazon's core leadership principles actually work.

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. So The Magic Loop is how to grow your career in almost any circumstance, even with a somewhat difficult manager. It does assume that you're working in some environment, normally as an entrepreneur or with a boss. But the basic idea of The Magic Loop is five steps and they're very easy. (00:06:01): The first one is you have to be doing your current job well. It's not possible to really grow your career if you're not considered at least performing at a solid level. Now, it doesn't mean you have to be the star on the team at this point, but what you can't have is your boss wishing that you were different. Like, "Ethan's not very good." So you have to talk to your manager and find out how you're doing and address any problems. So step one is do your job well. (00:06:31): Then step two is ask your boss how you can help. Speaking as a manager, and I've talked to hundreds of managers, very few people go and ask their manager, "What can I do to help you? What do you need?" And so just asking sets you apart, and it begins to build a relationship that we're on the same team, that I'm here as a part of your organization to make you successful, not just myself. (00:06:53): Step three is whatever they say, do it. So you dig a big hole. If you say, "What could I do to help you?" And they say, "Well, we really need someone to take out the tray sheets day," and you're like, "Oh, I didn't mean that. I wanted exciting work. I don't want to do sort of this maintenance work or whatever." So do what they ask, help out even if it's not your favorite work. (00:07:14): Once you've done that though, and maybe you do that a couple times, the fourth step is where the magic comes in. You go back to your manager and say, "Hey, I'm really enjoying working with you. I'm wondering is there some way I could help you that would also help me reach my goal?" And whether that goal is to change roles or get a raise or get a promotion, you say, "My goal is I'd really like to learn this new skill. Is there something you need that would also help me learn this new skill?" And the reason this works is managers help those who help them. It's just human nature. We all do that. (00:07:52): Generally, they're very open to meeting you halfway and saying, "Sure, I need this. We can rearrange it. We can find a way to meet your goals over time." Now for step four to work, you do have to know what is your goal, so you have to be clear on what it is you want. Well, that part's up to you. (00:08:15): And then step five is the easiest step of all. It's just repeat. So like lather, rinse, repeat with your shampoo. Step five is once you're working with your manager towards your goal and discussing where you're going, and you're helping each other, the magic of the loop is just go around and around.
turns.zh:
是的，当然了。“魔术循环”（The Magic Loop）是一种在几乎任何环境下提升职业生涯的秘诀，即便面对一位有些难缠的上司也不例外。它确实假设你身处某个工作环境中，通常是作为创业者或下属。但“魔术循环”的核心理念在于五个步骤，而且步骤非常简单。（00:06:01）：第一步是做好当前工作。若你连基本水平都达不到，就无法真正提升职业生涯。当然，这并不意味着你必须成为团队中的明星，但至少不能让上司希望你有所改变。比如，“伊桑表现不佳”。所以你要和经理沟通，了解自己的表现并解决问题。第一步就是做好本职工作。

（00:06:31）：第二步是主动询问如何能提供帮助。以经理的身份来说，我和数百位经理交流过，很少有人主动问：“我能如何帮助你？你需要什么？” 这种主动询问能让你脱颖而出，也能建立一种我们同属一个团队的信任感——我来这里是为了助你成功，而不只是为自己谋利。

（00:06:53）：第三步是无论对方说什么，都要照做。比如你问：“我能如何帮助你？” 对方回答：“我们真的需要有人负责收拾托盘。” 你可能回应：“哦，我不是这个意思。我想要更激动人心的工作。” 但还是要按要求做事，哪怕不是你最喜欢的工作。（00:07:14）：不过一旦你这样做了，或许重复几次后，第四步才是关键所在。你回到经理面前说：“嘿，我真的很享受与你共事。我想知道有没有什么办法能既帮到你，又能助我达成目标？” 无论目标是转岗、加薪还是晋升，你都可以说：“我的目标是学习新技能。你是否需要我具备的某项能力能帮助我掌握新技能？” 这个方法之所以有效，是因为经理会帮助那些帮助他们的人。这是人性使然，我们都会这样做。

（00:07:52）：通常，他们很乐意与你达成妥协，说：“好吧，我需要这个。我们可以调整安排。总能找到方法逐步实现你的目标。” 但第四步要奏效，你必须清楚自己的目标是什么，这部分就得靠你自己了。

（00:08:15）：最后第五步是最简单的。就像用洗发水洗头一样，反复操作即可。第五步是当你与经理朝着目标共同努力、交流发展方向并互相支持时，“魔术循环”的魔力就开始循环往复了。

turns.en: Yeah, okay. Very fair. So I called it The Magic Loop because I pioneered it with my audience a few years ago. My boss has asked me to do all these cool things, and I feel like I can't catch up, and I've already been promoted once and I need time to digest it." And it just seemed like it worked like magic. It worked in almost every circumstance. (00:09:15): There are of course exceptions where you have very exploitative managers who are like, "Oh, it's great. This is a path to all of that, because it's forming a partnership with your leadership to say, "Look, I'll help you, but I need you also to help me." And most good managers are very open to that.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。说得很在理。所以我把它命名为"魔术循环"，因为几年前我和听众们一起开创了这个方法。效果非常显著，很多人反馈说："怎么关掉这个功能？我现在完全应付不过来了。老板让我做各种酷炫的项目，可我根本跟不上节奏。虽说我已经升职一次了，但还需要时间消化这一切。" 它似乎真的像魔术一样管用，几乎在任何情况下都能奏效。（00:09:15）当然，也有一些例外——比如那些剥削员工的管理者，他们会说："太棒了。你工作更努力了，继续保持啊"，然后却什么都不为员工做。但这种情况很少见。那么这个方法的核心目标是什么呢？是帮助你在职业生涯中获得满足感。很多人对工作不满，很多人想晋升或加薪，但并非所有人都如此。有些人想转行，因为工作太无聊了。而这正是通往这些目标的路径，因为它是在与领导建立合作关系时说："看，我愿意帮助你，但你也要帮帮我。"大多数优秀的管理者对此都持开放态度。

turns.zh: 自从这个方法推出以来，有哪些方面需要补充、调整或帮助听众更好理解？我想肯定会有批评的声音，也会有很多人说："对，对，对。这个方法确实有效。"

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Two things I'd love to clarify. The first is many people ask me, "Why do I have to do this? Shouldn't my manager notice what I'm doing? Shouldn't my manager help with my career? Shouldn't my manager be planning for me?" And what I say about that is what your manager should do and $4 will get you a cup of coffee at Starbucks. (00:11:36): The point of this loop is it's in your control. It is true that a good manager would do all those things I just mentioned, but not all managers are good and some of them need some help. And the thing I would just say about The Magic Loop is it's in your control. (00:11:52): And so you can be upset that your manager isn't perfect, but move on from that and take control of your own situation. That's the first thing I'd say. The other big extension I would make is look, if you are a manager or a leader of any type, you can initiate The Magic Loop from your side, so you can talk to your employees and say, "Hey, what are your career goals? Would you like to form a partnership where you step up to new challenges and I help you get to your goals?" (00:12:26): I had a lot of success forming this kind of partnership with my employees, where as they saw growth and success, they really leaned in and like, "This system works. You're actually investing in me now. I'll work extra hard." And I'm like, "Yes, and we can grow your team or grow your opportunity," and it was very win-win.
turns.zh:
以下是您提供的英文文本的简体中文翻译：

有两件事我想澄清一下。第一，很多人问我：“为什么我必须自己做这些事？我的经理不应该注意到我在做什么吗？不应该帮助我规划职业发展吗？不应该为我制定发展计划吗？”对此我的回答是：你的经理应该做这些事，但星巴克一杯咖啡才4美元。（00:11:36）这个循环的关键在于，你完全可以掌控局面。诚然，优秀的经理会做好我提到的所有事情，但并非所有经理都称职，有些人还需要改进。而关于“魔术循环”，我想说的是：你完全可以自主掌控局面。（00:11:52）所以，如果你对经理的不足感到失望，别纠结于此，而是主动把握自己的职业发展。这是我想说的第一点。另一个重要延伸是，如果你是一位管理者或领导者，你也可以从自身出发启动“魔术循环”。你可以和员工沟通：“嘿，你们的职业目标是什么？愿意与我结成合作伙伴，一起迎接新挑战，实现共同成长吗？”（00:12:26）我与员工建立这种合作关系时收获颇丰。当他们看到自己的成长和成功时，会更加投入，说：“这个体系有效。你现在真的在为我投资了。我会加倍努力。”我回应：“没错，我们可以壮大你的团队，拓展你的发展机会。”这真是双赢局面。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To give people a little bit of social proof, you mentioned some of the folks you've worked with on this. Can you share some stories, or stats, or anything to help people understand how helpful this ended up being to folks you've worked with?
turns.zh: 为了给听众提供一些参考案例，您提到了与您合作过的一些人。能否分享一些故事、数据或其他案例，帮助听众理解这种方法对合作伙伴的实际帮助？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. I'll tell one story from each end of the spectrum. And what I mean there is entry-level people and then high level executive leaders. I had an entry-level person write me back and say, "Look, when I learned about The Magic Loop, I was at a company and not doing very well. I started applying it. They offered me a $30,000 raise and a bigger job. And I turned it down because I got hired at this other company that was offering me even more, and I went there. And they've promoted me also," and he was one of the people who wrote in and said, his exact words were, "A year ago I was made redundant." So he is in the UK, redundant is their word for laid off. "A year ago I was made redundant. I got this first job and I got an offer for an increased salary, and then I got the second job and I got an increase when I joined that was even bigger." And he was in that situation of, "Mow I need to sort of slow down and digest all of that." (00:14:05): On the complete other end, one of my best people I ever worked with joined my team at Amazon as what we would call an SDE II, which in Amazon is a level five employee. He grew with me kind of following this process to a senior engineer. Then he switched to management and ran a small team. Then he became a senior manager and he relocated with my organization. He opened a new office in another city, was eventually promoted to director running his own office of a couple hundred people. And this was over the course of about eight years. He went from a mid-level engineer to an executive with a team of 800 people. Now he was a very hard worker, but over this eight years we just saw all this progress. (00:14:56): And then eventually he moved on. He founded his own startup, sold that, and now works as an executive vice president at one of the major online banks. And so his career in some sense has exceeded mine, but during that eight year span, he just grew so much. And this is the process we followed.
turns.zh:
是的，当然可以。我会讲两个极端案例——一个是初级职场人士，另一个是高层管理者。有一位初级员工给我写信说："我刚加入公司时表现不佳，但学习了'魔术循环'后，公司不仅给我加薪3万美元，还升了职。但我拒绝了，因为另一家公司给我的待遇更高，最后我去了那家公司，现在他们还提拔了我。"还有人写道："一年前我被裁员了。第一份工作加薪后，第二份工作又涨了更多薪水。现在我需要放慢脚步，消化这些变化。"

（00:14:05）：另一个极端例子是我共事过的最优秀的员工之一。他加入亚马逊团队时是SDE II级别（相当于亚马逊的五级员工）。他跟随我的成长路径晋升为高级工程师，随后转入管理层，负责一个小团队，接着成为高级经理，跟着我的团队迁移至新城市，并最终晋升为管理数百人的部门总监。在这八年间，他从中级工程师成长为高管。如今他创立了自己的初创公司，成功退出并加入一家大型在线银行担任执行副总裁。他的职业生涯在某种程度上比我还要出色，但在这八年里，他的成长确实惊人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, those are excellent examples. What levels does this help you with? At what level is this most useful, and then does it kind of taper out it? I don't know if you get to VP level, do you still try using Magic Loop?
turns.zh: 哇，这些都是很棒的例子。这个方法对不同职级的人都有帮助吗？在哪个职级最有用？之后效果会逐渐减弱吗？我不知道达到副总裁级别后，是否还会继续使用'魔术循环'？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: So I think it works anywhere from the start of your career to pretty far into it. I think at my level, I finished my career as a vice president at Amazon. It does peter out in the sense of the active. And what I mean by that is you're still doing the same thing, but you don't have to talk about it. Your managers are expecting you to step up and recognize challenges. They're expecting you to ask for resources when you need them, and you don't sort of have this level of explicit conversation around, what can I help you with? They're expecting you to anticipate what's needed. (00:16:09): So in the newsletter we did together, I wrote about how over time, you go from asking your manager, "How can I help?" To suggesting to your manager, "These are some things I see that seem like they need to be done. Would you like me to do them?" To just seeing what needs to be done and sort of keeping your leader in the loop and saying, "Hey, I noticed that we have this problem. I fixed it. I noticed we have this opportunity. I've started program against it." I think at the executive level, it's much more you being proactive and just keeping your leader in the loop.
turns.zh: 我认为它适用于从职业生涯初期到中后期的任何阶段。以我个人经历为例，我在亚马逊以副总裁身份结束职业生涯。它的实用性确实会随职级递减，具体来说就是主动性逐渐降低。我的意思是，你仍在做同样的工作，但无需事事汇报。你的经理期望你主动发现挑战，主动申请资源，而非被动等待指示。（00:16:09）：在我们共同撰写的通讯中，我写到随着时间推移，你会从询问上司'我能帮什么忙？'，转变为主动向上司提出建议'我发现了这些问题，需要处理吗？'，再到主动发现问题并及时汇报。到了高管层级，更需要你主动出击，随时向上司汇报进展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think in the post, the way you described this step is this is advanced mode. Don't jump straight to this. Don't just start suggesting things, because you may get it wrong.
turns.zh: 我觉得你在帖子里描述的这个步骤属于高级模式。别直接跳到这步。别一上来就开始提建议，否则你可能会出错。

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Yeah, well, it's all a matter of rapport and trust. A huge part of career success is how much trust you have, mutual respect with your leadership. When they're confident that you're going to make the right decisions, they're confident to let you go. But yeah, when you're brand new or you're new to a manager, if you just jump in, you may either not work on the things they value or even find yourself working across purposes, and that isn't the right place to start.
turns.zh: 是啊，这完全关乎默契和信任。职业成功的关键在于你与上司之间能否建立充分的信任和相互尊重。当他们相信你能做出正确决策时，才会放心放手让你行动。但如果你刚入职，或者刚换了新上司，一股脑儿冲进去，要么做不到上司看重的事，甚至可能南辕北辙，这可不是个好的开端。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. Just to close out this conversation. You touched on this, but why is it that you think this is so important and effective? Why do you think this works so well? People may not recognize, "I see this is the key to this."
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。总结一下今天的讨论。你之前提到过这点，但你为什么觉得这点如此重要且有效？为什么你认为这个方法效果显著？人们可能不易意识到：“我发现这就是关键所在。”

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Well, I think it's two things. First, I mentioned how rare it is for managers to be offered help. If you're a manager, you'll recognize this. If not, feel free to talk to any manager, whether your own or somebody else. Ask them how much they worry and how much they feel overwhelmed and wish someone would give them a hand. Management can be a lonely job, because you feel like you're responsible for everything. So having an ally, it's just a huge weight off people's shoulders. (00:18:01): And then I think a lot about social engineering. The social engineering's here is just the simple, "You help me, I'll help you." It doesn't have to be exploitative, it's just we help those people who help us, and that's built into human survival. (00:18:18): And I think this loop works so well because it's just leaning a little bit into that behavior. So many relationships with managers are oppositional. You tell me what to do, and I'm kind of like a kid in high school who's trying to figure out how do I skip as many classes as possible and turn in as little homework and still get by with a D? That relationship won't build your career. (00:18:45): Some people approach their jobs as my goal is to do the least I can and still collect my paycheck. That's an approach if you're okay with where you are. It's not what I coach though. I assume people want to grow.
turns.zh: 嗯，我觉得有两个原因。首先，我提到过上司很少主动寻求帮助。如果你身为上司，就会深有体会。即便不是上司，也不妨去和其他上司聊聊，无论是自己的还是他人的。问问他们有多焦虑、多不知所措，多希望有人能帮把手。当上司这份工作很孤独，因为你觉得自己要对一切负责。所以有个盟友，真的能为人解压。（00:18:01）然后我常思考社交工程学。这里的社交工程很简单，就是“你帮我，我帮你”。不必带有剥削意味，就是我们帮助那些帮助我们的人，这本就是人类生存的本能。（00:18:18）我觉得这个循环之所以有效，是因为它恰到好处地顺应了这种行为模式。很多和上司的关系充满对抗。上司说“你按我说的做”，下属就跟高中生似的，想着怎么逃课、少交作业还能拿个D级成绩？这种关系不会助你事业发展。（00:18:45）有些人工作态度是“我只要尽可能少做事，照样领薪水”。如果你能接受现状，那倒也无妨。但这不是我所倡导的。我相信人们都渴望成长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so maybe it's just as a closing question, for people that are listening and want to start putting this into practice slash are stuck in their career and are just like, "Okay, I see. Here's something I can do." Could you just again summarize the loop briefly?
turns.zh: 好，那最后再总结一下，供正在听讲、想付诸实践，或者正卡在职业瓶颈、想“好的，我明白了，接下来该怎么做”的人参考。你能再简要总结一下这个循环吗？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Sure. Step one, make sure you're doing your current job well. The way I explain this is when you go to your manager and ask, "What could I do to help?" You don't want their answer, even if they don't say it quite so bluntly to be, "Do your F-ing job." You need to be doing that already. So be doing a good job. (00:19:34): And unfortunately, a good job is in the eyes of your manager in this case. You may think I'm doing great work, but if your manager doesn't, they're the ones you need to build as an ally here. (00:19:46): Once you have that, go ask how you can help, do whatever you're asked, and then go back to your manager and suggest or ask, "I would like to meet this goal. Can I keep helping you? What could I take on that you need that would also help me meet this goal?" And that's where you start to try to bring your two sets of aims together. What do you need done, how can I get to my goal? And let's do those things together. (00:20:11): And then you just repeat this loop. You build trust, you build the relationship. And with all good managers, and even a lot of moderate managers, they appreciate the help so much, they really lean into that.
turns.zh: 好的。第一步，确保你能把当前工作做得出色。我的解释是，当你去找经理问“我能怎么帮到你？”时，你不需要对方直接说“你他妈的做好本职工作”，但你确实应该已经在做好本职工作了。所以要先把工作做好。（00:19:34）：不幸的是，在这种情况下，经理眼中的“做好工作”可能和你自己的认知不一致。你可能觉得自己工作得很棒，但如果经理不这么认为，那你就需要把他当作盟友。（00:19:46）：一旦你确定了这一点，就去问如何能提供帮助，完成经理交付的任务，然后再回头问经理：“我希望达成这个目标。您能继续让我帮忙吗？您还有什么需要我协助的任务，能同时助力我实现目标？”这样你就能开始把自己的目标和经理的需求结合起来。他们需要完成什么任务，你又能如何达成自己的目标？然后一起行动。（00:20:11）：接着你就不断重复这个循环。建立信任，发展关系。只要是优秀的经理，甚至是普通经理，他们都会非常感激你的帮助，愿意与你深度合作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think there's two really important elements of this that you haven't even mentioned necessarily, that I think are part of the reason this works so well. One is this forces you and your manager to identify the gaps that are keeping you from the next level, which it's often vague, and then you get to a performance review, and then your manager's like, "Ethan, you're still not good on this and this and that," and you're like, "You never told me that that's the things you're looking for for me to get promoted." So I think there's this implicit, here's what you need to work on to get to the next level, which I think is part of step four. (00:20:53): And then you actually did touch on this that it's important to share your goal to your manager. Here's what I want. I want to get promoted. A lot of times they don't know that and you helping them understand, "Here's what I want, help me get there." It goes a long way. So there's a lot-
turns.zh: 我觉得这里面有两个很重要的点你可能没特别提到，但它们正是这个方法之所以有效的原因之一。第一，它迫使你和经理共同识别阻碍你晋升的差距。很多时候这些差距很模糊，直到绩效评估时经理才会说：“伊桑，你还是不擅长这个、那个、那个。”而你可能会说：“你从没告诉我这些是你认为我晋升必须掌握的技能。”所以这其实是在暗示：“这里是你需要改进的地方，这样才能晋升。” 这就是第四步的核心。（00:20:53）：然后你确实提到要和经理分享自己的目标。这很重要。“我希望晋升。”很多时候他们并不知道这一点，而你帮助他们理解：“这是我的目标，帮我实现它。” 这会产生深远的影响。所以还有很多——

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Managers often fall into the trap. They chose to become managers, so they assume one of two things about you. They either assume that you want to keep doing exactly what you're doing forever, just maybe make a little more money. (00:21:16): So you're an artist, you want to keep drawing forever. You're a lawyer, you want to keep writing contracts forever. Or they assume that, "Hey, I became a manager. I'm very proud of my career. That must be what you want." (00:21:29): And these assumptions are natural, right? We tend to view by default that our path is great and everyone would want to be us. Now of course, some good managers don't do that. But if you clarify and express your goals, you remove that ambiguity.
turns.zh: 经理们经常陷入误区。他们选择当经理，所以会对员工有两种假设。他们要么认为你想永远保持现状，只是赚多点钱。（00:21:16）：比如你是个艺术家，永远想画画。你是个律师，永远想写合同。或者他们会想：“嘿，我当了经理。我为自己的职业生涯感到骄傲。这肯定就是你想要的。” （00:21:29）：这些假设很自然，对吧？我们默认自己的路径很棒，每个人都想成为我们。当然，有些优秀的经理不会这样做。但如果你明确表达自己的目标，就能消除这种歧义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I actually had a period in my career where I specifically did not want to get promoted. I was very happy where I was, and I just wanted to keep doing this awesome IC role. Is that something at all you see where people are just like, "I'm good. I don't need to get promoted," and then is this helpful in that in any way or is it not as big a deal?
turns.zh: 我职业生涯中确实有段时间特别不想晋升。我在现有岗位上很开心，只想继续做这个很棒的IC角色。你有没有遇到过这种情况：有人说“我现在挺好的，不需要晋升。”那这对他们有帮助吗？还是说这没那么重要？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: So first, I reached a point in my career where I was no longer pursuing promotion either, and I wanted to do other things. So I've lived that myself and I've used the same loop, but I used it to go do what I wanted to say, "This is now what I want, and how do we get there? How do we create a role where I'm adding value appropriate to my level, but I'm doing this other work that's fun?" I moved into gaming and I really wanted to do that. (00:22:25): Second, I think it is still helpful because there's something you want probably. Maybe you want to work on different kinds of projects or maybe you want to work with a different higher performance team. Or maybe you want to rebalance your life and say, "Hey, I love what I'm doing, but how can I be a star performer for you but within these boundaries?" (00:22:47): So if you truly have the perfect job just as it is, you may not need The Magic Loop. But I know so few people if you're like, "Nope, there's absolutely nothing I could improve about my role."
turns.zh:
首先，我在职业生涯中达到了一个阶段，那时我不再追求晋升，而是想做些其他事情。我自己就经历过这样的过程，我也曾运用同样的方法，但这次我是为了去实现自己的目标——“这就是我现在想要的，那该如何达成呢？如何找到一个既能发挥我现有价值，又能让我做自己喜欢的、有趣工作的职位呢？” 于是我转行进入游戏行业，而这正是我的真心所向。（00:22:25）  
其次，我认为这种方法仍然有用，因为你很可能也有自己的目标。或许你想参与不同类型的项目，或许想加入更高绩效的团队，又或许想重新平衡生活，问自己：“我热爱现在的工作，但如何在现有框架内成为明星员工呢？”（00:22:47）  
所以如果你对现有工作非常满意，可能不需要“魔法循环”方法。但我很少遇到这样的人——他们会说：“不，我的工作完全无需改进。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I think that your point about your goal doesn't have to be promotion. It could be work on a different part of the org, try something totally... Maybe transition to a new function that could be part of your goal. Awesome. (00:23:09): Okay, so along the same lines of career progression, you work with a lot of senior manager types, kind of the level of L7 and one M2-ish, and you share with me that one of the most frustrating parts of their job in that specific portion of their career is they get stuck at that level and they don't move up, and it becomes really annoying, and they're not sure how to break out of that. What advice you share with folks like that, that may be listening?
turns.zh:
是啊，我觉得你的观点很对，职业目标不一定要是晋升。可以是尝试不同部门的工作，或者完全转行到新领域。太棒了。（00:23:09）  
好的，回到职业发展的话题。你与很多高级经理打交道，比如L7级别和M2级别左右的职位。你告诉我，他们在职业生涯中最头疼的问题之一，就是卡在当前级别无法晋升，这真的很让人沮丧，他们不知道如何突破现状。对于听众中可能遇到这种情况的人，你有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Yeah, so it's common to get stuck there, and there are a few reasons for it. First, there are a lot of senior managers. If you think of your average director, they may have six to eight reports. How many more directors are needed? So there's a choke point. (00:23:52): Second, that choke point is worse in the current economy, and in the past maybe a lot of companies, Amazon, Google, apple, etc., were growing very rapidly. And so it wasn't just you were waiting for some other director to leave. The teams were getting bigger. (00:24:07): I experienced this at Amazon, where over a nine-year period I went from managing six people to 800. And so I went from a senior manager all the way to a vice president, and I described I was, in some sense just riding the elevator. The elevator was going up, and as long as I managed to stay on it, I was going to arrive at vice president. (00:24:29): But the other thing that causes people to get stuck is the difference between a senior manager and a director is how you lead and the work you're doing. And you can get as far as senior manager by being really strong in your function and being really good at getting things done. As a director, and as a VP beyond that, it becomes much more about influence, coordination with others, and letting go of being in all the details yourself. And so senior managers really have to change some behavior. (00:25:03): I often reference the book by Marshall Goldsmith, What Got You Here Won't Get You There. Not only because it's a great book classically on this problem, but because the title tells the story. All the great traits that got you to this one level won't get you to the next level where you're more expected to be thinking in strategic terms, thinking longer term.
turns.zh: 是的，在这种情况下卡住是很常见的，原因有几个。首先，公司里有很多高级经理。如果你想想普通的总监，他们可能有六到八个下属。那么还需要多少个总监呢？所以这就形成了一个瓶颈。（00:23:52）其次，在当前的经济环境下，这个瓶颈问题更加严重。过去很多公司，比如亚马逊、谷歌、苹果等，发展得非常迅速。那么你不只是在等待其他总监离职，团队规模也在不断扩大。（00:24:07）我在亚马逊就有过这样的经历，九年间我从管理六个人发展到管理800人。所以我从高级经理一路晋升到副总裁，可以说这整个过程就像是搭电梯。电梯一直在上升，只要你能一直待在里面，最终就能晋升到副总裁的位置。（00:24:29）但导致人们卡住的另一个原因是，高级经理和总监在领导方式和工作内容上存在差异。高级经理晋升到这个职位，主要靠在本职领域表现出色、善于把事情做成。而到了总监及副总裁级别，更多的是要发挥影响力、与他人协作，以及学会放手让别人处理细节。因此，高级经理们确实需要改变自己的行为方式。（00:25:03）我经常引用马歇尔·戈德史密斯的《让你成功的不是过去的经验》这本书。不仅因为这本书对这个问题有经典的解析，更因为书名本身就道出了真相。那些让你晋升到当前职位的优秀特质，并不一定能助你登上更高台阶，因为在更高层级，你需要具备更长远的战略思维能力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So to someone that may be in that role today and they're not moving up, is there anything they can do? This point about just there's no roles for you, there's only so much you can do there, is the advice just wait until an opportunity arrives? Is it run this Magic Loop until something happens? Is there anything you can do?
turns.zh: 那么对于那些目前身处这个职位却停滞不前的人，有什么解决办法吗？当面临“公司没有适合你的职位”或者“你能做的已经做完了”这样的困境时，建议是等待机会降临吗？还是要一直循环往复直到有所突破？他们能做些什么呢？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: I would be honest with people and say some patience is required. At this level, there is some notion of, do we need a director? Do we need a vice president? Do we have a challenge at that level that needs that person? And so promotions at this level, I often teach have two components. The first component is can I eat and do that job? Am I qualified? Do I have the skills? But the second piece is, do we have such a job that needs that? (00:26:09): However, there is a lot you can do. A lot is in your control. And what is in your control is to start practicing those next level skills. Start working with your leadership on, where can I take on a strategic project? How can I become more of an inventor? I teach some about how to sort of systematically be inventive. It's not pure magic. Edison said it's 1% inspiration and 99% perspiration. You can learn the 99%, and the 1% isn't as hard then. So you start showing those next level traits. And as I describe it most succinctly, how do you make yourself the person who will be chosen out of the eight? (00:26:51): And you can be chosen, there are several ways to move up. Your boss can leave or be let go. They can be promoted to another role. But another way is I coach now, and I have several clients recently. I was just talking to a client yesterday, her two peers were let go. They were all the same level. Her two peers were let go and she was given their teams. And she expressed that her boss had been told, "You have too many senior managers for the size of your organization. We need to do some change in the organization, clean house, and put all your people under the folks who have potential." (00:27:32): Well, obviously she must be one of those people, because she still has her job and has more people and more to do. And unfortunately, her peers are shopping for new employment. So be that person, and that's where The Magic Loop comes in. Be that person.
turns.zh:
我会诚实地告诉大家，这需要一些耐心。在这个层级上，人们会思考：我们是否需要一个总监？是否需要一个副总裁？这个层级是否有挑战需要这样的人才？因此，这个层级的晋升通常有两个关键点：第一，候选人是否胜任当前职位？是否具备相关技能？第二，组织是否真的需要这样的人才？（00:26:09）不过，你还是能做很多事情的。很多事情都在你的掌控之中。关键在于开始磨练下一个层级的技能。比如，和你的领导探讨：我能接手什么战略项目？如何成为更具创新力的人？我会教授一些系统性创新方法。这并非魔法。爱迪生曾说：“灵感是1%，汗水是99%。99%是可以习得的，1%则没那么难。”所以要开始展现这些下一个层级的特质。用我最简洁的话来说，你要如何从八个人中脱颖而出？（00:26:51）晋升之路有多种可能：你的上司离职或被裁员；他们被调任其他职位。但还有一种方式——我现在指导的几位客户就是例子。昨天我刚和一位客户聊天，发现她的两位同级同事被裁掉了。他们原本处于同一层级。她的上司被告知：“贵公司规模与高级管理层数量不成正比。我们需要调整组织架构，优化资源，将所有潜力人才纳入核心团队。” 
（00:27:32）显然她是幸运者之一，因为她保住了职位，还接手了更多团队和更繁重的工作。而她的同事们只能另觅新职了。所以要成为这样的人，这正是“魔力循环”的精髓所在。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was just talking actually to a senior PM leader who pointed out that with this kind of lean environment of a lot of flattening of orgs and a lot of layoffs, that this is becoming increasingly hard. Exactly what you're describing. There's just less spots, because companies are running more lean, and so you just kind of have to wait. (00:28:06): I think part of this advice you just shared, which is classic do the job before you have the job makes all the sense in the world. Because once people see that you can do it, obviously they'll feel a lot more comfortable putting you in that position.
turns.zh: 我刚和一位高级项目经理交流，他指出，在当前组织扁平化、裁员频发的精益环境下，这种晋升之路愈发艰难。这正是你所描述的现状。职位空缺越来越少，因为公司在追求更精简的架构，所以只能等待机会。（00:28:06）你刚才分享的建议很经典——在获得职位前先做好本职工作，这完全说得通。因为一旦人们看到你能胜任当前工作，显然会更放心地把职位交给你。

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: And they'll be looking. I always remind people, as a leader, I want the best people under me I can have. It's not that I don't wish to promote you. If you think about my job, this helps people, right? I have selfish motivation to promote you. A lot of people think, "The bosses there holding me down." Well, maybe some bosses are, but why wouldn't I want stronger, more capable direct reports? Why wouldn't I want people under me who can do more of my job? Frankly, that's the only way I can do less of my job.
turns.zh: 他们会一直在观察。我总是提醒下属，作为领导者，我希望手下都是最优秀的人才。这并非不愿提拔你。要知道从我的角度看，这能帮助更多人。坦白说，我晋升你的动机是利他的。很多人认为“上司故意压制我”。或许有些上司确实如此，但我为什么不希望手下有更强、更有能力的直接下属？为什么不希望他们能承担更多我的工作？说实话，这才是我能减轻工作负担的唯一途径。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Plus this pressure you're always getting from your reports. So like, "Hey, I'm ready to get promoted, because this time"... You mentioned this word inventiveness, and I was just listening to Jeff Bezos on Lex Fridman, and I don't know if you heard this, but Jeff Bezos described himself most as an inventor more than anything else that he does. Is that something that you think about? Is that influenced by Jeff Bezos any way, that idea of being an inventor as a leader?
turns.zh:
另外，你总是会面临来自下属的压力。比如，“嘿，我已经准备好升职了，因为这次……”  
你提到了“创造力”这个词。之前我在听杰夫·贝索斯（Jeff Bezos）在Lex Fridman的访谈时，不知道你是否听过，他把自己描述为一个发明家——比起其他任何身份，这一点对他来说最为重要。你有没有想过这一点？你认为作为领导者，具备发明家的特质是否会受到杰夫·贝索斯的启发？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: I'll say a couple things about that. First, I know you talked to my old boss, Bill Carr, who wrote Working Backwards. What I don't know is if he shared with you that after he published it, he actually realized there was a better title. He wishes that he had called the book The Invention Machine, because what Jeff was trying to do with Amazon was create the most inventive company, the company that would systematically out-invent others. And so while Working Backwards is a great title, Bill and Jeff think they should have called it the Invention Machine. (00:29:47): When I joined Amazon, I did not think of myself as an inventor, but I saw that we had these leadership principles think big and invent and simplify that pushed on that. And I said, "I'm in trouble. I don't know how to do this." And I sat down and thought about that. What am I going to do? It seems like that's required. And I figured out how to become systematically inventive. So I now hold over 70 patents as one benchmark of inventiveness, and they were all created during my 15 years at Amazon. (00:30:22): And the way I did that, inventiveness actually isn't that hard. I teach about this. And to invent systematically, first you do need to be somewhat of an expert in whatever area you want to invent. So Lenny, if you and I say let's get together and we're going to invent cancer drugs, we have the problem that neither of us, as far as I know is a biologist, a doctor. We don't have the right background, we don't know what we're doing. So we would just be fumbling around I guess with a bathtub full of chemicals hoping. It's probably not going to work out that well. So you have to be something of a knowledgeable expert. (00:30:56): But then the second thing people don't do is they don't spend dedicated time actually thinking. They feel like, "Invention is just going to come to me." When I want to invent, I get away from all my devices. I go in a room with the problem I have, and I force myself to actually concentrate on what do I know and how can I invent? And the most straightforward way to invent is not to somehow come up with something completely new, but instead to put together two things that exist. (00:31:28): And so my example of this, I have a patent I talk about a lot for a drone delivery for Amazon, but the drone doesn't fly from the warehouse. Instead, a truck with no top drives slowly around the neighborhood, and the drones go back and forth from the truck. As opposed to the driver stopping at every house, you can have four or six drones hitting everything in the neighborhood. (00:31:55): And the way I came up with this idea is one day I was thinking about drones and delivery, but I loved military history. And so I was thinking also about an aircraft carrier and I was thinking, is there a way to have an aircraft carrier for drones? And from that, it was very quick for the light bulb to go on and say, well, what about a truck? (00:32:17): And so I have this patent, and we haven't seen this become reality yet. I'm waiting for my idea to become part of Amazon's drone delivery system, but I think ultimately it will.
turns.zh:
关于这点我要说几句。首先，我知道你和我的前老板比尔·卡尔聊过，他写了《倒退工作法》。但我不知道的是，他出版这本书后，其实意识到还有个更好的书名。他希望当初能把书命名为《发明机器》，因为杰夫在亚马逊的目标是打造最具创新力的公司，一个能系统性地超越他人的创新型企业。虽然《倒退工作法》是个很棒的书名，但比尔和杰夫都觉得他们本该用《发明机器》这个名字。

（00:29:47）我加入亚马逊时，并不认为自己是个发明家，但我发现公司有三大领导理念——“大胆思考、勇于创新、化繁为简”——一直在推动我前进。我当时想：“我遇上麻烦了。我不知道该怎么做。”于是我坐下来思考：该怎么办？这似乎是必须面对的挑战。后来我找到了系统性创新的方法。如今我拥有70多项专利，这可以作为我创造力的一个衡量标准，而这些专利都诞生于我在亚马逊的15年间。

（00:30:22）实现这一目标的方法其实并不难。我常讲这个理念。要想系统性地创新，首先得在你想创新的领域成为专家。比如，如果你和我说要一起发明癌症药物，但据我所知，我们俩既不是生物学家，也不是医生，缺乏专业背景，根本不知道该怎么做。只能是胡乱尝试。所以必须得有扎实的专业知识。

（00:30:56）但人们常犯的另一个错误是，不肯投入时间去思考。他们总觉得：“创新会自然降临。”我要创新时，会关掉所有设备，专心思考已知的知识如何能转化为创新。最直接的创新方式，不是凭空创造新事物，而是把已有的东西结合起来。

（00:31:28）举个例子，我常提到的亚马逊无人机送货专利。无人机不是从仓库起飞，而是装在没有顶篷的卡车上，缓慢行驶在社区里，这样无人机就能在卡车和地面之间往返。相比于司机挨家挨户送货，四到六架无人机就能覆盖整个社区。

（00:31:55）这个想法的灵感来源于我对无人机送货的思考，同时我热爱军事史。于是我联想到航母——有没有办法为无人机打造航母呢？很快我就灵光一闪：那用卡车怎么样？

（00:32:17）这个专利目前还没实现。我在等待我的创意被纳入亚马逊无人机送货系统，但我相信最终它一定会成为现实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is badass. I'm imagining returns come back to the truck. We're using that rope thing that just captures them with that little hook.
turns.zh: 这太酷了。我想象退货物品被送回卡车上。我们用那种能用小钩子抓住物品的绳索装置。

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Yeah. Well, there's no reason... Same thing. When you want to return something as opposed to taking it to the UPS Store or whatever, you just put it on your porch, and then on your phone, on your app, maybe you take a picture of it so that the drone can recognize the box or you put it in a designated spot, and you push a button and the drone takes your return away. Yes, there's no reason.
turns.zh: 是啊。不过没关系……道理都一样。假如你想退货，而不是把商品送到UPS门店之类的地方，你只需把商品放在自家门廊上，然后在手机应用里拍张照片，让无人机识别箱子型号，或者把商品放置在指定位置，再按个按钮，无人机就能把退货物品带走。确实没问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can't wait for that. And it takes your dog backs in it sometimes, part of it.
turns.zh: 我都等不及了。不过有时候无人机还会把你的狗带走，这也是个问题。

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: My dog's too heavy, thank you.
turns.zh: 我的狗太重了，谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: My dog's not. There's an owl in our backyard that we sometimes worry he is going to come grab our dog on. This idea of invention, this is really interesting. I didn't plan to talk about this, but for someone like say a PM on a team that wants to get better at invention, innovation, big thinking, is there a practice you find helpful here? Is it block off two hours, get a pen and paper, and just think about the specific two adjacent things working together?
turns.zh: 我的狗可不重。我们后院有只猫头鹰，有时我们还担心它会来抓走我们的狗。说到创新，这个概念真的很有趣。我本没打算讲这个，但对于那些想在创新、发明和大胆构想方面有所提升的团队成员来说，比如产品经理，有什么实用的方法吗？比如专门抽出两个小时时间，拿起笔和纸，思考两个相邻事物如何协同工作？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: So that's part of the process, is put in dedicated time. The interesting thing I would say is you don't need that much time. Two hours is great, but you only need two hours once a month. People think invention takes all this time. The thing is once you have one good idea, it often takes years to express that. (00:33:52): So you had the idea to have a newsletter. I know some of the history of your newsletter. You've been working on the expression of that idea for years now. Jeff and Amazon had ideas like, "Let's have Prime shipping." Well, Prime is still getting better and still being worked on. It's a 20 some year old idea. The Kindle a decade's old idea now still getting better. (00:34:16): So the point here is you don't need very many good ideas to be seen as tremendously inventive. Like Elon Musk, Tesla, he can kind of dust off his hands and be like, "I am now an Edison-like inventor." So he keeps doing it, but you don't need that many inventions.
turns.zh: 这就是创新过程的一部分，需要专门投入时间。我想说有趣的是，时间不需要太多。两个小时很棒，但每月只需一次就够了。人们总觉得创新需要大量时间。关键是，一旦你有了好点子，往往需要数年时间才能将其付诸实践。（00:33:52）：比如你曾有过创办新闻通讯的想法。我了解你新闻通讯的部分历史。你为这个想法努力了多年。杰夫和亚马逊也有过类似想法，比如“推出Prime会员服务”。但Prime至今仍在不断优化完善。这是个二十多年前的创意。Kindle也是十年前推出的创意，如今仍在改进。（00:34:16）：所以关键在于，你不需要太多好点子就能被视为极具创造力的人。比如埃隆·马斯克、特斯拉，他能随口说一句：“我现在是个像爱迪生一样的发明家。”然后继续行动，但其实不需要太多发明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This touches on something else Jeff Bezos shared on the podcast that most of his innovation and work is in the optimizing phase. It's not the here's the idea, it's the making it cheaper, and better, and faster. And that's where most of the good stuff comes from. In this point of Tesla, Elon had this idea, and now the hard work is actually making it scalable and cheap enough for people to use, not just an electric car.
turns.zh: 这也呼应了杰夫·贝索斯在播客中提到的观点——他的大部分创新和工作都处于优化阶段。不是提出一个点子，而是让它更便宜、更优质、更高效。这才是大多数优秀成果的源泉。以特斯拉为例，埃隆最初有这个想法，现在关键在于让它具备可扩展性，让普通人也能负担得起，而不只是生产一辆电动车。

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: With the idea of Jeff saying that invention is really a lot of the incremental and optimization, I completely agree with that. To invent well, you need a base idea, but then there's so much of the work is making that idea real. (00:35:15): And again, Prime is a great example of this. The Amazon Prime program was a great example of, okay, we want fast free shipping. We want this program. That was a one-time idea that they did build, but now Prime has expanded. First it was two-day in the US, then one-day in the US, now it's same day in the US. But also they added Prime Video, Prime Music, Prime Gaming. There's actually something like 25 things you get free with Prime. Most people have no idea, because you get free photo storage and this ongoing list. And all of that is that incremental optimization to make it better, better, better, better. And of course Jeff's goal, which you probably heard him say, was to make Prime a no-brainer, to where you would be irresponsible really not to be a member.
turns.zh: 杰夫说创新实际上是大量渐进式改进和优化，我完全赞同这一观点。要想成功创新，首先需要有一个基础构想，但后续的工作重点在于将这个构想变为现实。（00:35:15）再举个例子，亚马逊Prime会员计划就是一个典型案例。最初他们提出“我们想要快速免费送货”这个构想，随后不断升级服务：从美国两日达，到一日达，再到当日达。同时还增加了Prime Video、Prime Music、Prime Gaming等附加服务。目前Prime会员可以免费享用约25项服务，多数人对此知之甚少——从免费照片存储到持续更新的功能清单，无不体现着不断优化迭代的精髓。当然，杰夫的目标是让Prime成为“无需犹豫的选择”，让人们意识到不加入会员实在是失策。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know you have an awesome Jeff Bezos story that I want to get to, but before we do that, one more question along this line of career advice and progression. So I read somewhere that you've interviewed over 2,500 people over the course of your career. And so kind of going back to the beginning of a career, or at least getting a job, what have you found is most helpful in standing out as a candidate when you're interviewing, and essentially getting hired? What advice do you have for people that may be going through an interview process right now?
turns.zh: 我知道你有关于杰夫·贝索斯的精彩故事，等下再聊。但在此之前，我想继续探讨职业建议与发展的话题。我读到你职业生涯中采访了超过2500人。那么，回溯职业生涯初期或求职阶段，在面试中脱颖而出、成功获聘的最关键要素是什么？对于正在经历面试流程的人，你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: There's a lot of evidence that suggests that the number one and two factors in any interview are appearance and enthusiasm. And it doesn't mean you have to be beautiful, but show up somewhere looking like you're interested in the job, not in your pajamas. And most importantly, be enthusiastic. People want to work with people that want to work with them. So if you seem very judgmental of the company and like you have to sell me on it, you're going to turn them off. I look at every interview of whether or not I really want this job, I might've decided I don't want the job. I still want the offer. (00:37:10): And so I come to any interview I do leaned in and talking about how excited I am to be a part of this opportunity and what I know about the company. Beyond those cosmetics, the biggest thing I see particularly at higher levels is people talk about what they have done but not why it mattered. They don't talk about the impact. (00:37:32): See, a leader is not hiring someone to just do work. They're hiring someone because they have a problem or a need. And so if you can show them, "Look, here's the things I've done that have made a difference. Here's the things I've done that have helped my past employers where I've had an impact." So I didn't just do work. That makes you a worker. Someone who has an impact is more of a leader. (00:37:57): And leader doesn't need to mean people manager, just a higher level, that I have done something that solve the big problem, and here's how it changed the company or customer outlook. That's what I'm looking for in an interview, is are you bringing me an understanding of the business that shows you contributed to the business, or are you just telling me how hard you worked?
turns.zh: 大量证据表明，面试中最重要的两个因素是外在形象和热情。这并不意味着你必须长得漂亮，但至少要看起来对这份工作感兴趣，而不是穿着睡衣去面试。最重要的是，保持热情。人们希望与愿意为他们工作的同事共事。所以如果你显得对公司很挑剔，仿佛需要说服对方接受你，那就适得其反了。每次面试前，我都会自问是否真心想要这份工作，甚至可能决定不想要这份工作，但还是希望获得录用通知。（00:37:10）因此，我每次面试都会全情投入，谈论自己对参与这个机会的兴奋之情，以及对公司的了解。除了这些表面功夫，较高层级职位最显著的特征是人们只谈及自己的工作成果，却不解释其价值所在。他们不谈论影响力。（00:37:32）要知道，领导者招聘员工并非只是为了完成任务，而是因为存在问题或需求。因此，你必须向他们展示：“看，我做过这些有影响力的工作，帮助过过去的雇主，创造过价值。” 这样你才不是普通打工者，而是有影响力的人才。（00:37:57）领导者不一定意味着是人力资源经理，而是更高层级的人才——他们能解决重大问题，改变公司或客户的看法。这就是我面试时关注的重点：你是否能让我了解你的业务贡献，还是只是在吹嘘自己的勤奋？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. On that first piece, now that most interviews I imagine over Zoom, in terms of enthusiasm and looking professional, is there anything you've found that people may not be thinking about in those two buckets?
turns.zh: 太棒了。关于第一点，我想说在大多数远程面试中——无论是从热情度还是专业形象来看——有没有什么大家可能忽略的关键点？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Yeah. Show the person full-time dedication. So unless you really don't have any choice, don't take an interview from a car, don't have your camera off. Eye contact is still a real thing. Body language is still a real thing. Gestures like I'm making now with my hands, they're part of your presentation. (00:38:53): So be fully present and try to project through the camera a little bit of I'm excited to be a part of this and I appreciate the opportunity. I often tell people the best way to prep for an interview might be a good night's sleep and a pot of coffee, that being fully engaged and energetic is a huge lever.
turns.zh: 有的。要向对方展现出全职投入的状态。除非万不得已，否则别在车里接受面试，别关掉摄像头。眼神交流和肢体语言依然很重要。比如我现在用手比划的手势，这些都是你展示形象的一部分。（00:38:53）所以要保持专注，试着通过镜头传递出“我很兴奋能参与这次面试，也很感激这个机会”的感觉。我常跟别人说，准备面试的最佳方法可能是睡个好觉，再来一杯咖啡，保持充沛的精力和热情才是关键。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. And I think basically, the feedback there is don't over obsess with the content. There's a lot of value in just how you come across.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我觉得核心要点就是别太纠结于内容本身。你的整体表现才是最有价值的。

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Yeah, 100%.
turns.zh: 完全赞同！

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me tell you about a product called Arcade. Arcade is an interactive demo platform that enables teams to create polished on-brand demos in minutes. Telling the story of your product is hard, and customers want you to show them your product, not just talk about it or gate it. That's why product four teams such as Atlassian, [inaudible 00:39:49], and Retool use Arcade to tell better stories within their homepages, product change logs, emails, and documentation. (00:39:56): But don't just take my word for it. Quantum Metric, the leading digital analytics platform created an interactive product tour library to drive more prospects. With Arcade, they achieved a 2x higher conversion rate for demos and saw five times more engagement than videos. On top of that, they built the demo 10 times faster than before. (00:40:14): Creating a product demo has never been easier. With browser-based recording, Arcade is the no-code solution for building personalized demos at scale. Arcade offers product customization options, designer approved editing tools, and rich insights about how your viewers engage every step of the way. Ready to tell more engaging product stories that drive results? Head to arcade.software/lenny and get 50% off your first three months. That's arcade.software/lenny. (00:40:44): Now let's take a little trip to failure corner. This is something that I do more and more on this podcast, talk about people's failures in their career and their learnings. And apparently you have a great story of failing the great Jeff Bezos and surviving to tell the tale. Could you share that story?
turns.zh: 让我跟你介绍一个叫Arcade的产品。Arcade是一个互动演示平台，能让团队在几分钟内创建精良且符合品牌风格的演示文稿。讲述产品故事并非易事，而客户希望你展示产品本身，而非只是空谈或设置门槛。这就是为什么Atlassian、[未听清 00:39:49]和Retool等产品团队会用Arcade在主页、产品变更日志、邮件和文档中讲述更精彩的故事。（00:39:56）但别只听我说说。领先的数字分析平台Quantum Metric通过创建互动产品演示库，成功吸引了更多潜在客户。借助Arcade，他们的演示转化率提升了两倍，互动量比视频高出五倍。最重要的是，演示制作速度比以往快了十倍。（00:40:14）创建产品演示从未如此简单。基于浏览器的录制功能，让Arcade成为大规模构建个性化演示的无代码解决方案。Arcade提供产品定制选项、设计师认可的编辑工具，并全程追踪观众互动数据。准备好讲述更吸引人的产品故事并推动业务成果了吗？访问arcade.software/lenny，即可首月享五折优惠。（00:40:44）现在让我们来聊聊失败案例。这是我在播客中越来越常做的事，分享人们职业生涯中的失败经历以及从中获得的启发。显然，你有个和杰夫·贝索斯共事失败却最终成功的故事。能分享一下吗？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: I do. It's both a highlight and a low light. So I had been at Amazon about six years. I had become a director, and I was responsible for launching Amazon's app store. (00:41:14): And so we were building an Android-based app store to go on Google phones and eventually on the Kindle tablets. And we got to launch day. And at that time, Jeff used to write a letter introducing new products. He would write a letter that said, "Dear customers, today Amazon's proud to launch blah blah, blah, and it's got these great features and I hope you really enjoy it. Thanks Jeff." And we would take down all the sales stuff on www.amazon.com and that letter would fill the whole screen. (00:41:48): And so he had written a Jeff letter, and this Jeff letter emphasized a particular feature of our product that he really liked. So that something that made it a little different. (00:42:00): And that specific thing was we had a button called test drive that you could click on and it would open the app in a simulator in your web browser, so you could check out the app and interact with it before putting it on your phone. So he thought this was really cool and he was all about it. (00:42:19): Well, my team had built all this technology. We had test drive working. It was kind of a hard piece of technology if you think about simulating any of thousands of arbitrary apps. And we worked all night to launch it, and it wasn't quite working at 6:00 AM. We were still debugging. (00:42:38): Now you know engineers very well. And I'm sure most of your listeners know about engineers, even if that's not their discipline. We always think we're this close to finding the last bug. (00:42:49): So about 6:15 AM, I get a message from Jeff that says, "Hey, I woke up, where's the letter?" Because it was supposed to go live at 6:00 AM, right after the markets in New York would've opened at 9:00 AM Eastern. And he says, "Where's the letter?" And I write him back and I say, "Well, we're working on a few problems." And what I'm thinking in my head is, "Get in the shower, get in the shower. I just need 20 minutes, get in the shower."
turns.zh: 确实如此。这既是亮点，也是低谷。我在亚马逊工作了大约六年后，晋升为总监，负责推出亚马逊应用商店。（00:41:14）：当时我们正在开发基于安卓系统的应用商店，准备上线谷歌手机和Kindle平板电脑。到了上线日那天，杰夫（Jeff Bezos）习惯用信件介绍新产品。他会写一封信，内容大致是：“亲爱的用户们，今天亚马逊很自豪地推出……这款产品，具有诸多出色功能，希望大家喜欢。杰夫敬上。” 我们会把亚马逊官网上的促销信息撤下，整页只显示这封信。（00:41:48）：杰夫写了一封信，重点强调了我们产品中他特别喜欢的某个功能。这让产品显得与众不同。（00:42:00）：具体来说是我们开发了一个名为“试驾”的按钮，用户点击后能在网页模拟器中预览应用，这样他们就能在安装前先体验功能。杰夫觉得这功能超酷，对此特别上心。（00:42:19）：我们团队打造了这项技术，试驾功能已成功开发。但模拟数千款随机应用是个技术难关。为了按时上线，我们通宵调试，早上6点时技术仍不稳定。（00:42:38）：你们应该很了解工程师吧。我相信大多数听众即使非技术出身也对工程师有所了解。我们总觉得离找到最后一个漏洞就差一步了。（00:42:49）：早上6点15分，杰夫发来消息：“嘿，我醒了，信件呢？” 原定6点上线，紧接着纽约股市将于东部时间上午9点开盘。他问：“信件在哪儿？” 我回复：“我们还在排查几个问题。”心里却想：“快去洗澡，洗澡！只要20分钟，快去洗澡。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For Jeff to get in the shower.
turns.zh: 让杰夫去洗澡。

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Yeah. And 30 seconds later, I have an email back that says, "What problems?" And at this point I have to start explaining, and I end up explaining that we're having a problem with a database, and we're debugging this database problem. And he's like, "Wait, there's a database in your design? We're trying to eliminate all Oracle databases and move to AWS. Why do you even have this?" And he is just getting more and more frustrated and angry. (00:43:49): And he starts copying in my boss, and my boss's boss who's with Jeff Wilke, the CEO of retail. And they start asking me questions. And it's just this snowballing, but 7:30 in the morning, Jeff is clearly angry. And there's this list of other people waking up and feeling like, "Well Jeff is angry, so my job is to be even more angry," and it's just raining in on me.
turns.zh: 是啊。 30秒后他回邮件问：“什么问题？” 这时我不得不解释，原来是数据库出了问题，我们正在调试。他接着问：“等等，设计里有数据库？我们不是要淘汰Oracle数据库，转用AWS吗？为什么还用数据库？” 他越来越生气。（00:43:49）：他开始叫来我的上司和上司的上司——零售业务CEO杰夫·威尔克（Jeff Wilke）。他们开始质问我。整个局面像滚雪球般恶化，但早上7点半，杰夫明显怒不可遏。其他人醒来后也被卷入风暴，觉得“杰夫都发火了，我的任务就是比他更火大”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh man.
turns.zh: 天啊。

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: So what did I do? The interesting thing is what do you do when the future richest man in the world is mad at you? He wasn't quite richest man in the world yet, but he was headed there. (00:44:26): So the first thing I did was I owned it. I said, "Yes, it's not working. It's my fault. I will deal with it." I took ownership. And the second thing I did was start updating him very proactively and saying, "Here's where we are." 8:00 AM, "This is exactly where we are. This is what we're going to do and the next hour, and this is when you'll get your next update. I will update you again at 9:00 AM, so here's our plan." (00:44:55): And even though Jeff had sort of lost trust in me, like it's down, and it's not right, and I'm mad, given that he agreed with the plan, he was willing to give me 60 minutes. And then I would update him again and say, "Okay, this is what we've done and this is what we're going to do, and we'll update you again at 10:00 AM." So I was buying life one hour at a time. (00:45:17): Now the other thing I did, and this is a good thing about Amazon, as more and more leaders got copied into this angry thread, they started reaching out in back channel and saying, "We've all been under Jeff's Eye of Sauron, we know it's miserable. What can we do to help?" And essentially Andy Jassy's organization, which was AWS at that time, and his CTO, a guy named Werner Vogels said, "You're having a database problem, let's get you some principal engineers from the AWS database team." (00:45:54): And these principal engineers showed up at 9:00 AM roughly, and they looked at our design. We had made some fundamental mistakes in our database usage and they said, "It's too complicated to fix this. We're just going to give you 500 AWS machines so that your crappy design will run anyway. That's the immediate fix." And I'm like, "Okay, well I guess if you have 500 databases lying around because you're AWS, it's a great solution," and that's what they did. (00:46:27): So the next step is we fixed the problem. A bunch of us worked together very hard to get the problem all fixed. Now it took all day, and Jeff was still frustrated because the opportunity to sort of control the messaging and the media by having his letter up had passed. People had noticed our launch and the articles had been written, and so Jeff was still very mad. (00:46:52): So we fixed the problem, but Jeff now had no trust in us. The weekend went by. He was using the system looking for bugs because he is like, "This team's not reliable now. Ethan's not reliable. I better check it myself." So you have the CEO checking on you. (00:47:11): And he found a problem and emailed me like Saturday night at 9:00 like, "I was doing this and it broke." And luckily I was able to tell him exactly what happened by 9:30. Anyway, the next part of the story is that following week, I had a meeting with him on another topic. (00:47:32): So I was part of this small group that was trying to figure out how to build a competing browser. You may not remember, but Amazon had a browser called Silk for a while. And I was invited to this meeting, but I wasn't a critical participant. So you may know this idea from Scrum where they say some people are pigs and some are chickens, and the chickens are sort of observers. I was a chicken in this meeting, and that turns out to be a great analogy because I was thinking, should I chicken out and not go? I could skip this meeting with the CEO who's angry at me. But when I had that thought, I realized if I can't face the CEO, I'd better pack my desk. That's the end. (00:48:13): So I went to this meeting early, and Jeff always sat in the same chair, so I knew where he would sit when he came in. So I sat down right next to his chair and I thought, "I don't know, let's find out." (00:48:24): And so the meeting goes by, and of course in my mind Jeff is totally ignoring me, not even looking at me. But I think that's just me projecting, because remember I wasn't central to the meeting. (00:48:35): So at the end of the meeting, everybody gets up to leave. He turns and looks at me and says, "So how are you doing? I bet it's been a hard week." And I thought, "Oh, okay, we're going to talk." And I said, "Yeah," I just sort of answered him with, "Of course it's been hard, but here's what we're doing and here's what we're going to do in the future." And we had a very human conversation. And I didn't believe Jeff would've forgotten that I let him down, but it was clear he had forgiven it. (00:49:05): So I was still going to have to, as it turns out, re-earn his trust. But the thing I did that's key for people to learn from is it's really easy to flame. He had been flaming me, writing angry emails. Angry emails are easy. Sitting three feet from someone and being angry with them face-to-face is hard. And when faced with, I can either start ranting at this person who reports to me, or I can say something nice, he chose to say something nice, and that rebuilt our relationship. (00:49:42): So the end of the story is two years later, I was promoted to vice president. So even though I had failed the CEO on this very public launch where he was very definitely mad at me, I re-earned the trust, I showed I had learned the lessons of how to launch more reliably without outages, and I was promoted. (00:50:07): And so I share that story because I think what I want people to understand is if I can get away with publicly failing one of the richest and most famous inventors on earth, and then get promoted and finish my career at Amazon very successfully, you can dig out of any hole. You just have to manage it right.
turns.zh:
接下来我该怎么做呢？有趣的是，当未来世界首富对你发火时，你该怎么办？他当时还不是世界首富，但他正朝着这个目标迈进。（00:44:26）所以我首先承认了自己的失误。我说：“是的，现在系统出问题了。这是我的错。我会解决的。” 我主动承担了责任。接下来，我每隔一小时就主动向他汇报进展。早上8点，我说：“现在情况就是这样。我们接下来要做什么，接下来一小时内完成，10点再向你汇报。” （00:44:55）尽管杰夫对我失去了信任，觉得情况糟糕透顶，怒气冲冲，但鉴于他同意了我的方案，他还是给了我60分钟的缓冲时间。然后我每隔一小时汇报一次，说：“好的，我们已经完成了这些工作，接下来要做什么，10点再向你汇报。” 这样我每小时就为他争取到一次缓冲时间。

（00:45:17）另外，我做了一件事，这也说明了亚马逊的优点。随着越来越多的高管被卷入这场愤怒风暴，他们开始私下沟通：“我们都曾在杰夫的‘索伦之眼’下瑟瑟发抖，深知这种处境有多痛苦。我们能帮什么忙？” 安迪·贾西领导的AWS团队及其首席技术官沃纳·沃格尔斯主动介入，说：“你们的数据库设计有问题，给你们派几个AWS数据库团队的首席工程师。” （00:45:54）这些工程师大约在上午9点到场，审视了我们的设计。我们在数据库使用上犯了根本错误，他们说：“改起来太复杂了。我们直接给你500台AWS实例，让你那破设计也能运行。” 我回应：“好吧，如果AWS有500台闲置的数据库实例，那真是绝佳的解决方案。” 他们照做了。（00:46:27）接下来我们解决了问题。团队全力以赴，最终在当天下午修复了问题。然而杰夫仍怒气冲冲，因为他本可以通过提前发布信件控制舆论和媒体关注，但机会已经错失。人们注意到了我们的发布，文章已经见诸报端。（00:46:52）问题解决了，但杰夫对我们失去了信任。周末过去了，他持续监控系统，寻找漏洞，因为他觉得：“这支团队现在不可靠。伊桑不可靠。我最好亲自检查。” （00:47:11）周六晚上9点，他发邮件说：“我在操作时出错了。” 幸好我能在9点半准确告知他故障原因。接下来的一周，我和他就另一个议题开会。（00:47:32）我参与了一个小团队，试图研发一款竞争浏览器。可能你们不记得了，亚马逊曾推出过Silk浏览器。我受邀参加了这个会议，但并非核心参与者。Scrum中有个说法：有些人是积极分子，有些人是旁观者。我在这次会议中属于旁观者。这是个绝佳的比喻，因为我犹豫要不要临阵退缩。跳过这场与愤怒CEO的会面？但当我产生这个念头时，我意识到若连CEO都不敢面对，那我就该收拾行李走人了。这就是结局。
(00:48:13)：所以我提前去参加了那个会议，杰夫总是坐在同一把椅子上，所以我知道他进来后会坐哪儿。于是我坐在他椅子旁边，心想：“不知道试试看能发现什么。”  
(00:48:24)：会议进行了一阵子，当然在我看来，杰夫完全无视我，甚至都不看我。但我觉得这只是我自己的臆想，毕竟我在这个会议上并不处于核心位置。  
(00:48:35)：会议结束时，大家都起身离开。他转过身看着我，说：“你最近怎么样？我敢打赌这周一定很艰难。”我心想：“哦，好吧，看来我们要聊聊了。”然后我说：“是啊。”就这么随口回答：“当然很艰难，但接下来我们要这么做。”我们进行了一次很自然的交谈。我本以为杰夫会记恨我让他失望，但很明显他已经原谅了。  
(00:49:05)：结果我还是得重新赢得他的信任。但关键是，人们要学会如何化解矛盾。他之前一直在对我发火，写愤怒的邮件。发火容易，但当面和对方对峙很难。当面对时，我要么对下属发脾气，要么说些友善的话。他选择了后者，这重建了我们的关系。  
(00:49:42)：故事的结局是，两年后我被提拔为副总裁。尽管我在那次公开的发布会上让CEO大发雷霆，但我重新赢得了信任，证明了自己从容应对发布事故的能力，最终获得晋升。  
(00:50:07)：我分享这个故事，是想让人们明白：如果我能在全世界最富有、最著名的发明家面前公开失误，最终仍能成功晋升，在亚马逊圆满结束职业生涯，那么任何困境都并非不可逾越。关键在于正确处理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an amazing story. So there's a lot of lessons that I want to pull on here. One is just if you get caught in a situation like this where something completely fails, what I took down as you were talking, one is admit, yes, this is a huge problem, own it. This is like, don't try to deflect. (00:50:47): Two is the way I describe what you did here, is something I call prioritizing and communicating, where you prioritize, "Here's what we need to do," and then communicate. "Here's our priorities." And I love that you have this every hour, "Here's the latest, here's the latest." So make people understand you are on it and you'll continue to keep them updated. I imagine one of the worst fears is I have no idea what's happening here. I'm going to go in and start micromanaging.
turns.zh: 这真是个了不起的故事。所以我在这里想总结几条经验。首先，如果你遇到像这样事情完全失控的局面，我在你讲话时记下的关键点是，要承认问题确实存在，勇于面对。千万别试图推卸责任。（00:50:47）其次，我把你的做法归结为两点：一是优先排序和沟通。你先明确“我们需要做什么”，然后传达“这些是我们的优先事项”。我很欣赏你每小时汇报最新进展的做法，让大家清楚你在推进工作，会持续更新信息。我相信最令人担忧的情况之一就是，员工完全摸不着头脑，领导就会亲自插手微观管理。

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: You're exactly right. I'm trying to hold off micromanagement. I'm trying to give them, "Okay, I believe with this and I can wait an hour," and then I can wait an another hour because that team seems to be on it. So I'm trying to rebuild trust one hour at a time, and avoid having three or four levels of management all come in and start helping.
turns.zh: 你说得太对了。我正努力避免微观管理。我会告诉团队：“好的，我相信你们能处理，我可以等一小时。”然后再等一小时，因为那个团队看起来已经在处理了。所以我试图一小时一小时地重建信任，避免三四层管理层同时介入帮忙。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Then I love this other piece of advice of meet them in person, try to take it offline essentially, which I know you did later. But that's such a good point that it's hard to be as mad, and angry, and flamey in person. People are just going to be like, "Okay, I get it. Let's try to figure this out." Amazing. Is there anything else? Those are the three that I took away. Just like if you're caught in that situation in the moment, is there anything else that you found to be really helpful?
turns.zh: 然后我很赞赏你当面沟通，尽量把事情私下解决。我知道你后来也这么做了。但这确实是个好方法，因为面对面交流时人们很难发脾气、发火。大家只会说：“好的，我明白了。我们一起想办法解决。”太棒了。还有其他建议吗？这三个是我总结的。如果你当下正身处这种局面，还有什么其他真正有用的方法吗？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: I mean, work hard and fast, right? You do have to fix the problem. My team had been up all night. I had to start sending people home to sleep in shifts. We had to pull in all this help. And so it was a very hard weekend. (00:52:10): When you have a mistake, it's on you to pull out the stops, even if it's uncomfortable to recover from it. And again, this is not the time to be like, "Well, it's the weekend now, and my team, we'll hit it Monday." I'd have been out the door so fast, I would've had the comic Wile E. Coyote skid marks as I bumped down the street. So I would say that's important. It's part of showing ownership.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，要迅速行动，努力解决问题。我的团队整晚没睡。我不得不开始让员工轮班回家休息。我们不得不调集所有资源。这真是个艰难的周末。（00:52:10）当你犯了错误时，必须全力以赴解决问题，哪怕恢复过程中会很痛苦。这时候可不是说“周末到了，团队周一再处理”的态度。我当时肯定会冲出门去，那速度就像卡通人物威利·艾尔·科伊特从山上滑下来一样急不可耐。所以我觉得这很重要。这是展现责任担当的一部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other part of this is something I went through for a while when I was starting to become a more senior leader is I had a lot of imposter syndrome, and this fear that if I messed up, everything would crumble. People would see that I don't actually know what I'm doing, and I'm not really ready for this level of seniority. And so there's this fear of one big mistake, it's over. Clearly this was an example of a huge mistake and it was not over for you. Is there any lessons there that you take away of you can mess up and still do well, even if it's this level of mistake?
turns.zh: 另外，我在晋升为更高级领导时也经历过一段时间的冒名顶替综合症，担心一旦出错，一切就会崩塌。人们会觉得我根本不知道自己在做什么，根本不配担任这个级别的职位。所以我深知一个重大失误就意味着一切结束。但显然这次失误并没有终结你的事业。这里有没有什么经验值得借鉴？即使犯了大错，你依然能出色完成任务，哪怕是这种级别的错误？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: I think a lot of people in my position would've quit. They would've let the shame... I was just a little bit bullheaded where I'm like, "Yeah, I messed up. But I know I'm still a good person and a good worker. Yes, I made a mistake, but I'm going to move on." Part of the story I haven't told that you might enjoy is I mentioned that Jeff Wilke was Jeff's number two at that point. Jeff Bezos, number two person, and he was my skip level. (00:53:38): Well, during this process, he came physically into our offices and he wanted to talk to me, and my manager who was vice president said, "Hey Jeff, this is my team. I own it. If you have any criticism, say it to me. You don't mean to talk to my team." And Jeff Wilke said to my boss, whose name was Paul, "Paul, that's excellent leadership. I really appreciate what you're doing. Please step out of the way. I want to talk to Ethan. You're doing a great job, Paul. Now step aside." And then he kind of read me the riot act. (00:54:15): And the rest of that funny story is I was so happy with how well my meeting with Jeff Bezos went, I patted myself on the back and like, "I'm going to go face Jeff Wilke now. I'm going to schedule a meeting with him and do the same thing. I've got this down." (00:54:31): So I go to meet with Jeff Wilke, figuring I'm going to run the same playbook. I'm going to look him in the eye and all will be forgiven. And Jeff Wilke looks at me and says, "Ethan, when you launched this, did you know you were gambling with the result? Did you know it might not work?" And I said, "Yes. We had a media commitment to launch on that day, and I thought shooting for the date was more important than perfect certainty." (00:54:55): And he said, "Well, two things. First, you were wrong. You were wrong to prioritize date over our reputation. You let Amazon down in public and that was a mistake." He said, "Second though, at least you knew you were gambling. If you hadn't known you were gambling, we'd be discussing your departure." And I'm like, "Okay." Here I thought I was rolling in this meeting like I'm going to run my relationship playbook. And he's evaluating whether or not to keep me. (00:55:25): The bullheadedness is even after he had told me he had been considering firing me, I'm like, "Well he isn't. So I'm just going to go forward." And a lot of that stubbornness of sure I made a mistake, but I'm not going to live in shame about it, I think is what people can take away. I think a lot of people feel they're more dead in the water than they are. (00:55:53): Because everybody makes mistakes, right? I mean Jeff and Fire Phone, that'll be an albatross around his neck. Jeff and Fire Phone will be a phrase of anybody who knows Amazon for the rest of his life.
turns.zh: 我觉得很多处在我这种境地的人都会选择退出。他们会被羞耻感压垮……但我就是有点固执，心里想："是，我确实搞砸了。但我知道自己仍然是个好人，也是个优秀的员工。是，我犯了错，但我会继续前进。" 故事中还有个我没讲过的细节，你可能会感兴趣——我提到杰夫·威尔克（Jeff Wilke）当时是杰夫·贝索斯（Jeff Bezos）的得力助手，而杰夫·贝索斯是贝索斯集团的二号人物，他是我的直属上司。（00:53:38）：在处理这件事过程中，杰夫·威尔克亲自到我们办公室找我谈话。我的副总裁上司说：“杰夫，这是我的团队。我负责这里，要是你有意见就冲我说，不许找我的团队。” 杰夫·威尔克却对我的上司保罗说：“保罗，你的领导风格很棒。我很欣赏你的做法。但请让开，我要和伊桑谈话。你做得很棒，保罗，现在让开。” 然后他开始对我严厉批评。（00:54:15）：接下来的有趣故事是，我对和杰夫·贝索斯的会面非常满意，自鸣得意地想：“现在去面对杰夫·威尔克。我要安排个会面，照搬同样的策略。肯定没问题。”结果杰夫·威尔克看着我说：“伊桑，你启动这个项目时，知道自己是在拿结果赌博吗？你知道可能失败吗？” 我回答：“知道。我们对外承诺当天上线，我觉得赶在期限前发布比追求完美更重要。” 他说：“首先，你错了。你把期限置于声誉之上，让亚马逊在公众面前难堪，这是个错误。” 接着他说：“不过至少你知道自己在赌博。要是当时你不知道，我们现在就该讨论你的离职问题了。” 我说：“好吧。” 我原以为自己会像在会上照搬沟通策略一样得心应手，但他却在评估是否要留用我。（00:55:25）：即便他已经说过考虑解雇我，我还是固执地说：“好吧，那他没解雇我。我就继续前进。” 那种“我确实犯了错，但我不会因此羞耻”的态度，我觉得大家能从中领悟到很多。很多人觉得自己已经无路可走了，但其实并非如此。（00:55:53）：毕竟谁都会犯错，对吧？比如杰夫和Fire Phone项目，那可是他一生的污点。只要提到亚马逊，人们都会记得这段黑历史。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, we talked about it on the Working Backwards podcast, and why didn't Working Backwards work for the Fire Phone, we talked about it. I love that these quotes and lines are so seared in your brain. You can remember it like word for word exactly what-
turns.zh: 是啊，我们在《Working Backwards》播客上讨论过这个问题，关于Fire Phone项目为什么失败，我们也聊过。我很高兴这些引语和台词在你脑海中如此深刻。你能一字不差地回忆起每个细节——

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Well, I've relived that moment many times.
turns.zh: 嗯，我多次重温那一刻。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then just along the lines of working your way out of the hole, is essentially what you did just succeed for two years and do great, and that was the key there?
turns.zh: 然后就是摆脱困境的过程，本质上就是你成功了两年，表现出色，这才是关键吧？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: No, I think I did have to learn. I've always been sort of an operational cowboy, meaning I like to go fast and loose. I prioritize speed, and I really had to step back and say, "Okay, Amazon at this level and scale doesn't like that." So I've taught myself a new phrase which was fear the New York Times headline. Be aware that if Amazon is down, it goes up on every news website immediately. And so if Amazon has some kind of mistake, it's on Wall Street Journal and CNN. (00:57:07): And so as a leader, I had to think, is what I'm doing going to generate a New York Times headline? Because if it is, I'd better be really careful. And that's what I taught myself is you can't be paralyzed, but I taught my whole team, we don't want to be in the New York Times for the wrong thing. And that was the lesson
turns.zh:
不是，我觉得我确实需要学习。我一直有点像个"行动派"，喜欢行事迅速、随心所欲。我把速度放在首位，但后来不得不停下来反思："好吧，亚马逊在这种规模和层级下，可不喜欢这种作风。" 于是我自学了一个新理念——"敬畏《纽约时报》的头条"。要知道，如果亚马逊宕机了，各大新闻网站会立即跟进报道。若亚马逊出了什么差错，《华尔街日报》和CNN也会迅速报道。

（00:57:07）作为领导者，我必须审视自己的行为是否会引发《纽约时报》的头条。若真会如此，我最好谨慎行事。这就是我教给自己的道理：不能因噎废食。但我也向整个团队强调，绝不能因为错误的决策登上《纽约时报》头条。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along the lines of lessons, last question here, what's something that you took away from the way you approached it that you should have changed or should have done differently, that you've done differently since? Obviously don't... You mentioned this idea of don't promise a date that you're not that certain you're going to hit. I guess is there anything along those lines?
turns.zh: 再谈经验教训，最后一个问题：从你的处事方式中，你吸取了哪些本该改变或调整的教训？比如，你提到过不要承诺一个自己不确定能达成的上线日期。还有其他类似的教训吗？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: I have two things here. First, Amazon loved in the past, they loved surprise launches. They love the idea of we're going to be quiet, quiet, quiet. Because basically it was a reaction I think to Microsoft where they felt Microsoft always talked about what was coming and then pushed the dates back. And so there was this whole thing about vaporware. And Amazon wanted to be the other way, which is we won't say anything and then it will just be there. The problem I came to say is the biggest thing I learned with surprise launches is that you're surprised by what doesn't work. (00:58:23): And so I shifted the approach to let's do a lot of beta testing. We always, even if others don't agree quite and say, "You're right, we're not going to have a surprise launch." Some of our beta testers, even if they sign NDAs are going to leak. And that's a better outcome than launching something that doesn't work. That's one lesson. (00:58:46): The other lesson is this thing that broke in front of Jeff Bezos, ultimately it was a new college graduate engineer who wrote that code. And he had been left alone to write part of our user interface, but he had written it in such a way that it didn't scale. Now we didn't give him any help or oversight. We left him on his own, because we were busy focusing on other pieces of the problem. (00:59:20): And shortly after the disaster, he left the company. And the mistake I made was not reaching out to him and really reassuring him of, "Yes, you wrote the bug, but that's not on you. The system failed you and we don't see you. Bugs happen." (00:59:38): So the thing I regret in this whole thing is not realizing that even though no one in the team ever yelled at him or whatever, he knew it was his bug, and he obviously saw me and others sort of taking a beating. And so he left, and I wish he hadn't done that. And I wish more than that I had stepped in. I didn't realize what he was feeling.
turns.zh:
首先，亚马逊过去很喜欢惊喜上线。他们追求保持沉默的策略，避免提前透露信息。这其实是对微软的反击——微软总爱吹嘘即将推出的产品，却一再推迟上线时间，导致产品泡汤。亚马逊则反其道而行之，选择在行动中验证市场反应。

但我发现惊喜上线最大的问题在于，失败的往往是那些意料之外的东西。于是我转向了大量测试策略。即便其他人不同意，坚持"不搞惊喜上线"，我们的测试人员也会签保密协议泄露消息。这总比上线失败强得多。

另一个教训是，杰夫·贝索斯面前出问题的工程师，竟是一位刚毕业的新人。我们把他独自负责用户界面开发，却没提供任何支持。（00:59:20）灾难发生后不久，他就离职了。我的失误在于没有安抚他："代码出错不是你的错，是系统出了问题。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting, the lesson there isn't catch that person sooner, and notice these links in the chain that may break. But it's more just be there for that human that have this challenge, that people may not be focusing on.
turns.zh: 这让我意识到，团队成员即使没被公开批评，也能感受到压力。当事人需要被理解和支持。

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Because we lost a good person, and he probably felt very bad about it. And we all feel bad when we make mistakes. That can't be prevented. But he felt undue responsibility I think, and that I really regret.
turns.zh: 毕竟我们失去了一位好人，他对此深感自责。当我们犯错时，所有人都会感到内疚，这无法避免。但我认为他背负了过多的责任感，这让我深感遗憾。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is actually a really good example of ownership. You mentioned this term ownership and that connects to... Amazon has these leadership principles. I think there's 14 of them. One of them is around ownership. And apparently you helped craft the actual language for that principle, which I think is a huge deal with Amazon. I imagine very few people have a say over how to define, and describe, and say these principles. Could you just talk about this principle that you contributed to, how it came to be that you helped actually write it?
turns.zh: 这实际上是关于责任担当的一个绝佳案例。你提到了“责任担当”这个术语，这与亚马逊的领导力原则息息相关。我记得亚马逊有14条领导力原则，其中一条就围绕责任担当展开。显然，你参与了这条原则的实际措辞制定——要知道，在亚马逊，极少有人能参与定义、阐释和表述这些原则的工作。你能否谈谈你参与制定的这条原则，以及它是如何诞生的？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Amazon is now kind of on its fourth version in my mind, maybe there's more. But its fourth major revision of its leadership principles over its 25 plus year history. (01:01:18): And when it was going from version one to version two, Jeff and his leadership team sat down together. And actually in version one, there were three different lists. They were leadership principles and core values, and something else I don't remember. And they were like, "Three lists is stupid. Let's make one list." (01:01:36): Well ownership, the term had been a part of one of those lists, but when they merged everything, they took it out. And this guy Jeff Wilke I mentioned, the number two and the leader of retail, he brought a bunch of us a bunch of his directors. He brought the proposed list to us in a meeting and said, "Hey, this is the proposed new version, do you have any comment?" And we all sat around and talked and said, "Where's ownership? Ownership is missing." So we told him, he said, "Look, ownership is missing. We think it should be there." And he said, "Well, why don't you propose a draft?" (01:02:15): And so about a half dozen of us sat around and roughed out a draft of how we felt ownership should be written. And I proposed these six words, which are, "An owner never says that's not my job." Maybe that's seven words. (01:02:36): So I propose this specific language as a part of it and we sent off this draft. And months go by, we hear nothing. And then one day the leadership principles are announced and ownership is back in. It's been modified, but that, "An owner never says that's not my job," is a part of the leadership principle, and it's remained to this debt. (01:02:58): And what I love about that is because Amazon has one and a half million employees who live by these leadership principles, it's probably the most impactful thing I've ever written.
turns.zh: 在我看来，亚马逊如今已是第四版领导力原则了。（01:01:18）在其25年多的发展历程中，亚马逊对领导力原则进行了四次重大修订。（01:01:36）从第一版到第二版时，杰夫和他的领导团队曾召开会议讨论。第一版中有三个不同的清单——领导力原则、核心价值观，还有第三个我记不清了。他们觉得三个清单太麻烦了，于是合并成一个。（01:01:36）“责任担当”这个术语原本属于其中一个清单，但合并时被删掉了。我提到的杰夫·威尔克（Jeff Wilke），亚马逊零售业务的二号人物和负责人，带着一群董事来开会。他向我们展示了拟议的新版本，并问道：“你们有什么意见吗？”我们围坐讨论：“责任担当呢？责任担当没了。”于是我们告诉他：“看啊，责任担当没了。我们觉得应该加进去。” 他说：“那你们起草一份提案吧。”（01:02:15）于是，我们约六个人围坐在一起，草拟了我们心目中责任担当应有的表述。我提出了六个字：“负责人从不说‘这不是我的工作’。”可能这算七个字。（01:02:36）我把这段具体表述作为草案的一部分提交。几个月过去了，杳无音信。后来有一天，新版领导力原则公布了，责任担当又回来了。虽然经过了修改，但“负责人从不说‘这不是我的工作’”这句话仍是领导力原则的一部分，至今仍在沿用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. So those seven words are the most impactful thing you've ever written. I love that and I totally get that. I'm looking at the principles right now and it comes right at the end of that principle. We'll link to the 14 leadership principles. Is there another principle that you really love or one or two? I don't know. It's probably hard to pick your favorites.
turns.zh: 哇。所以这七个字是你写过最有影响力的东西。我很欣赏这一点，也完全理解你的感受。我现在正在看这些原则，它们就在这条原则的末尾。我们会附上14条领导力原则的链接。还有其他你特别喜欢的原则吗？比如一两条？我不知道。可能很难选出最喜欢的吧。

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: I'm a huge proponent of bias for action. Bias for action says speed matters in business and many decisions are reversible. And so it's important to go faster. (01:03:41): And I think people don't understand that in a competitive environment, being right is good, but being quick is necessary. Because if there are 10 startups working on an idea, some of them will gamble, and they'll make bad gambles, and they'll go out of business. But some of them will gamble and make an early bet and be right. And if you are not moving quickly, you'll be beaten by the people who maybe got lucky. (01:04:05): And so you've got to have a process that values speed, values, what can we do today? What can we commit to today? So I really like bias for action. Now that is what got me in trouble with Jeff, right? I was willing to gamble. So it has to be in balance, but that's my other favorite.
turns.zh:
我非常推崇行动偏见。行动偏见认为，在商业中速度至关重要，许多决策都是可以调整的。因此，必须加快行动步伐。（01:03:41）：我认为人们不理解，在竞争环境中，正确的决策固然重要，但快速行动才是关键。因为如果有10家初创公司都在研究某个创意，其中一些公司可能会冒险尝试，甚至会做出错误的决策，最终倒闭。但另一些公司会抓住先机做出早期决策，并最终获得成功。如果你行动不够迅速，就会被那些运气好的竞争者超越。
（01:04:05）：因此，你需要建立一个重视速度的流程，思考今天能做什么？今天能做出哪些承诺？所以我真的很喜欢行动偏见。不过这让我和杰夫·贝索斯闹了矛盾，对吧？我愿意冒险。所以必须找到平衡，但这是我最喜欢的理念。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Again, the Jeff Bezos interview with Lex Fridman, he was talking about how with Blue Origin, with the way Amazon, he thought about Amazon is customer obsession. That was the core goal and differentiator of Amazon. With Blue Origin, he wants it to be decisiveness. It's basically leaning into this bias for action fully, which is really interesting.
turns.zh: 再说杰夫·贝索斯接受莱克斯·弗里德曼采访的那部分。他谈到在蓝色起源公司，以及亚马逊的经营方式。他认为亚马逊的核心目标和竞争优势是以客户为中心。而在蓝色起源公司，他希望强调的是果断决策。这其实就是完全拥抱行动偏见的做法，非常有趣。

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: I saw that part of the interview and I thought, "Wow, that's exactly right." Because again, rockets blow up and they have people on them. You've got to get it right, but you also have to keep moving, because there's always one more thing you can safety test. So how do you balance it?
turns.zh: 我看了那部分采访，心想：“哇，真是说到点子上了。” 因为火箭发射可能会出故障，火箭上还有人。你必须确保安全，但同时也要不断前进，因为总有新的安全测试要做。所以如何平衡两者呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's interesting. With rockets, that's the one that you pick. It's pretty bold to be all move forward kind of thing. So this principle, again, going back to ownership, so you basically suggested this phrase, "You didn't hear anything," and all of a sudden it becomes part of the whole thing. Did that feel weird that they never told you, or I don't know if they gave you credit for that, or it's like, no, it's great?
turns.zh: 是啊，这很有意思。蓝色起源的案例就是你选择了这种全速前进的策略。这确实需要很大的勇气。所以回到所有权这个概念，你提出了“你什么都没听到”这样的短语，然后突然它就成了整个项目的一部分。他们从未告知你这一点，这让你觉得奇怪吗？或者说他们可能给了你荣誉？还是说他们觉得这没什么大不了的？

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Yeah, I wouldn't even claim credit for it, except I kept a copy of the email that says, "Ethan thinks it should say blah." I have the written proof. Because it's not about the credit. I'm very happy and proud that those words were kept. But in Amazon, I doubt if Jeff knows I wrote those words. It's not like I've ever told him, "Hey, do you know you kept my words?" That's not appropriate. It's just a fun anecdote. (01:05:55): And it does show, I guess something people can learn from that though, you can influence way up in a company if your ideas are good. And also, when we challenged, Jeff Wilke was a strong opinionated leader who didn't necessarily always love being challenged. (01:06:15): And so when we first told him, "Well, we think you're missing ownership," he was like, "You're staying that the whole S team can't get its leadership principles right?" I mean it wasn't exactly that way, but he was very much like, "Well, is this really necessary? Why do you think it's necessary?" And his challenge to us to write it was kind of framed as, "Well if you're so sure it's good, show us." But again, I'm stubborn and I'm like, "All right, let's write it." And we did.
turns.zh:
是啊，我甚至不愿居功，不过我保留了那封邮件副本，上面写着“伊桑认为应该写成这样”。我有书面证据。但这无关荣誉。我很高兴也很自豪这些话被保留下来。但在亚马逊，我怀疑杰夫是否知道是我写的。我从未跟他说：“嘿，杰夫，你知道你保留了我的话吗？”这不太合适。这只是个有趣的轶事。
（01:05:55）：不过这确实说明了一个道理：如果你提出的想法好，你就能在公司高层产生影响力。还有，当我们挑战现状时，杰夫·威尔克是一位固执己见的领导者，他并不总是乐于接受挑战。（01:06:15）：所以当我们第一次告诉他：“嗯，我们认为你忽视了所有权问题。”他反问：“你是说整个S团队都无法正确理解领导力原则吗？”我的意思不是完全那样，但他的质疑语气类似：“嗯，这真的有必要吗？为什么你觉得有必要？”他让我们写下文档时，语气就类似：“好吧，如果你这么确定，那就写出来吧。” 但我很固执，就说：“好吧，我们写吧。”然后我们就写了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's funny. That's not a great example of leadership where he is like, "Hey guys, I need your feedback on this thing. But no, don't actually tell me anything's wrong."
turns.zh: 这挺有意思的。这可不是那种领导力典范——他不会说：“嘿，伙计们，我需要你们对这个提案反馈一下。”

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Well, yeah. I mean for a bunch of directors to kind of critique the work of people two levels higher, he wanted it, but then he's sort of naturally resistant to it if we're kind of poking at his baby.
turns.zh: 嗯，是啊。我是说，一群导演去批评比他们高两级的人的作品，他本想这么做，但当我们对他的心血之作指手画脚时，他自然会感到抵触。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's unlikely that there's something huge missing and it turns out there was.
turns.zh: 不太可能有重大疏漏，结果偏偏就出问题了。

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I guess just on these principles, people may not know this, but this is where disagree and commit comes from. It's actually have backbone, disagree, and commit. We talked about this on the podcast about working backwards. I also love leaders are right a lot. That comes up a lot and I love that, to be successful, you need to be right. You can't just project confidence. You can't just be in a bunch of meetings and ship things. You need to be right to be successful.
turns.zh: 我猜基于这些原则，人们可能不知道这一点，但这正是"先同意再反驳"的由来。其实核心在于要有骨气，先不同意，再行动。我们在播客上讨论过逆向工作法。我也特别喜欢"领导者往往是对的"这种观点。这个观点经常被提起，我很认同——要想成功，你必须正确。不能只是装出自信，不能只是参加一堆会议然后仓促上线。要想成功，就必须有真知灼见。

turns.speaker: Ethan Evans
turns.en: And that one's been rewritten to carefully say, it's always interesting what is the history of the edits, which you wish you could see the edit history on these. That one got modified to say something about leaders actively work to disconfirm their beliefs. (01:07:58): And the key there is it was trying to get at the idea that you've got to be very open and always be questioning, "Yes, I think I'm right, but what's the new evidence? What am I learning?
